body:
I'm happy that if you think this is required, it should be fine (as it should be low cost). :+1: 

For future reference though, the PR info seems thin on the ground ..  is it possible you could expand on it to what problems it solves (presumably stutter), how you found it to be an issue, what the reasoning is etc?

I've added a description. Also, I've marked this as draft because this is not a full fix, as I realized later. It looked like a complete fix because this already makes the racey situation much less likely, and so I couldn't reproduce the issue in my subsequent attempts. However, more extensive testing revealed the issue can still show up. Therefore, I'll look more into this until I'm sure the fix is 100% good.

I don't know if 3.x suffers from the same race conditions that 4.x seems to have had since forever basically, but since physics queries go through `PhysicsDirectSpaceState*D`, which completely bypasses any sort of command queue, you end up with some pretty sketchy race conditions when doing physics queries while running the server on a separate thread, since the server thread is unblocked as soon as `PhysicsServer*DWrapMT::sync` is done, allowing it to (erroneously) ~~step the physics simulation~~ mutate shapes/bodies/whatever in parallel with the rest of the physics processing (and thus physics queries).

We merged #109591 for 4.5 to at least block the server thread until `PhysicsServer*DWrapMT::end_sync` is done, thereby resolving the concurrency race, but that (perhaps unsurprisingly) didn't solve the actual data race, resulting in some weird issues, so now the more pragmatic option seems to be to just bypass the command queue entirely during physics processing, leaving only `PhysicsServer*D::step` to run asynchronously: #117268

@mihe I didn't comment on your 4.x PR, but as far as I know physics is the exception in that it provides methods to query the server during regular use.

The other servers (in 3.x anyway) are essentially one way, and any functions for reading back are marked as unsuitable for use in games because they will either cause a stall / or be inaccurate / out of sync. Some queries might be ok for things that don't change much, but others are bound to cause problems.

I would be asking the question of _why_ there are functions that query physics, and whether they are a good design, given Godot's client / server queue paradigm.

If they can _mutate_ the physics outside the queue, that sounds very dodgy indeed.

> as far as I know physics is the exception in that it provides methods to query the server during regular use.

I'm not super familiar with the other servers, but yes, the `PhysicsDirectBodyState*` and `PhysicsDirectSpaceState*` classes would largely be that exception I guess, along with a few other methods.

> I would be asking the question of _why_ there are functions that query physics, and whether they are a good design, given Godot's client / server queue paradigm.

To be clear, when I say physics queries, I'm mostly referring to ray-casts, shape-casts, overlap checks, that type of thing, i.e. what `PhysicsDirectSpaceState*` exposes, which is obviously ubiquitous in games. The `PhysicsDirectBodyState*` class being exposed is much more questionable though.

I do think both of these classes are an odd quirk in Godot's API. I can only assume that they came about long before there was the option to run the server on a separate thread, presumably as a performance optimization. As you say, they don't really fit into the client/server architecture either.

> If they can _mutate_ the physics outside the queue, that sounds very dodgy indeed.

The space queries can't (or at least shouldn't) mutate anything, but any mutating command you queue up during `_physics_process`, like `PhysicsServer*::shape_set_data`, is free to be processed on the server thread right away, while you move on to call `PhysicsDirectSpaceState*::intersect_ray` (potentially implicitly through the `RayCast*` nodes) which would be reading the state now being mutated by `shape_set_data`.

@mihe, thanks for your insight on this. I acknowledge my last iteration of this PR would still race. I've pushed a new version that implements the stall-command-pumping-thread pattern. At least in my tests (on Windows, iOS and Android) everything seems in order. I still have to figure out the CI issue, but otherwise this is ready for review.

**UPDATE:** I might have figured it out.

I've pushed an overhauled version of the changes, including some simplifications and, more importantly, additional fixes: added missing initialization (the ultimate reason why CI was not passing on Linux) and additional handling of command queue bypass situations.

I'm going to test it a bit more over the next days, but I'm already quite confident about the changes.
